name: Kinesiology tape posture taping
lead: Kinesiology tape posture taping is the use of stretchy, adhesive elastic tape, commonly sold as Kinesio tape or K-tape, across the shoulders and upper back to cue a more upright shoulder position. In looksmaxxing and posture circles it is discussed as a way to counter rounded shoulders and forward-head posture, which people link to a more favorable side profile and neck line.

The tape itself is a thin cotton strip with acrylic adhesive that can stretch to roughly 140% of its length and is marketed for pain and sports injuries. It was developed in the 1970s by Kenzo Kase, a Japanese-American chiropractor, and became widely visible after it was supplied to athletes at the 2008 and 2012 Olympics [1].

Systematic reviews of kinesiology tape for pain and performance have generally reported small or trivial effects and little advantage over other treatments or sham taping, as summarized on Wikipedia [1]. Sources available for this article do not include a controlled trial of tape specifically as a posture-correction method for appearance.

Up to about 4 days per application, per manufacturer-style descriptions [1]

paras: Kinesiology tape is a latex-free elastic cotton tape with a heat-activated acrylic adhesive, designed to approximate the thickness and elasticity of skin. When applied under stretch it recoils and tugs gently on the skin [1].

For posture, practitioners and users apply strips across the upper back or shoulder blades so that the tape tension is felt when the shoulders round forward, intended as a reminder rather than a mechanical brace.

Kenzo Kase developed the tape in the 1970s and his company sells it under the Kinesio brand. Its popularity rose after the product was donated to athletes at the 2008 Beijing and 2012 London Olympics, and beach volleyball player Kerri Walsh wearing it on her shoulder in 2008 is often cited as a visible moment [1].

In 2017 the company KT Health settled a Massachusetts class action over its marketing for 1.75 million US dollars, agreeing to refunds and to drop claims such as injury prevention while adding a disclaimer that the tape was not clinically proven for all injuries [1].

Manufacturers and users have proposed that the tape lifts the skin to decompress fascia, improves lymphatic flow, reduces pressure on pain receptors, or improves proprioception, meaning the awareness of body position. Critics cited by Wikipedia say these claims lack supporting evidence [1].

A 2012 review found trivial pain relief in sports injuries; a 2014 review found negligible effects on muscle strength; a 2015 review found benefit over no treatment for chronic musculoskeletal pain but not over other treatments; and a later review of chronic low back pain found short-term pain reduction without a significant advantage over sham taping for other outcomes [1]. The proprioception-cue explanation is the one most aligned with posture use, but no study among the sources reviewed tests it for appearance.
No studies found on kinesiology tape as a posture or appearance intervention. Studies of the tape for musculoskeletal pain and sports performance exist and are summarized above [1].
The sources reviewed do not describe adverse effects. As with any adhesive, skin irritation is a general consideration.

timeline.event: Tape appears prominently at the Beijing Olympics [1].
Tape supplied to athletes at the London Olympics [1].
KT Health settles a marketing class action [1].

card.summary: Elastic tape across the upper back as a shoulder-position reminder; the tape's pain evidence is thin and posture-for-looks is untested.
card.note: No studies found on taping for posture or appearance.

quick.overview:
Posture taping means sticking elastic kinesiology tape across the shoulders and upper back so that you feel a tug when your shoulders slump. Some people use it hoping for a straighter, more open posture.

The tape was developed in the 1970s and became famous at the Olympics. Reviews of it for pain and performance report small effects, and no study among those found tests it for posture appearance.
quick.mechanism: The idea is sensory feedback: the tape pulls on the skin when posture slips, which proponents say improves body awareness. Manufacturers have also claimed effects on fascia and lymph flow, which critics say lack evidence.
quick.risks: Reported risks are minor and not detailed in the available sources; skin irritation from adhesive is a general consideration. In 2017 the leading brand settled a lawsuit over marketing claims.
